title: Subgroup
body:
A subset $H \subseteq G$ that is itself a [[Group]] under $G$'s operation. Written $H \le G$.

You do not check all four axioms. Associativity is inherited from $G$ for free, so the work is:

**The subgroup test.** $H \le G$ if and only if
1. $H$ is non-empty (in practice: $e \in H$),
2. $H$ is closed under the operation,
3. $H$ is closed under inverses.

**One-step version**, which is what you actually use: $H$ is non-empty and $ab^{-1} \in H$ for
all $a,b \in H$. For a **finite** $H$, closure alone is enough, because repeatedly multiplying
$a$ by itself must eventually cycle back and hand you $a^{-1}$.

This is the same shortcut as the three-condition subspace test in [[Vector Space]], and for the
same reason: the ambient structure supplies the laws, the subset only has to not leak.

## Examples

| $G$ | $H$ | |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathbb{Z}$ under $+$ | $n\mathbb{Z}$, the multiples of $n$ | every subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$ is one of these |
| any $G$ | $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself | the trivial subgroups, always present |
| $S_n$ | $A_n$, the even permutations | see [[Alternating Group]] |
| $D_n$ | the rotations | index 2, so half the group; see [[Dihedral Group]] |
| $GL_n$ | matrices of [[Determinant]] 1 | |

A non-example worth having: the odd permutations are **not** a subgroup, because odd times odd
is even. They fail closure, and they do not contain the identity.

## Generated subgroups

For $a \in G$, the set of all powers $\langle a \rangle = \{\dots, a^{-1}, e, a, a^2, \dots\}$ is
a subgroup, the **cyclic subgroup generated by $a$**. Its size is the order of $a$. This is the
cheapest way to produce subgroups and the reason [[Cyclic Group]] comes next: every element of
every group generates one.

More generally $\langle S \rangle$, the subgroup generated by a subset $S$, is the smallest
subgroup containing $S$, which is the intersection of all of them. Compare **span** in
[[Vector Space]]: same construction, "everything reachable from these using only the operations
you have".

## The constraint that makes them useful

Subgroups cannot be any size they like. [[Lagrange's Theorem]] says $|H|$ divides $|G|$, so a
group of order 12 has no subgroup of order 5, and there is nothing to search for. That is what
turns "find the subgroups" from an open-ended hunt into a finite check, and it is why [[Coset]]
is worth building first.
